summary:
Our project aims to develop an interactive, web-based scientific exhibition that makes scientific information easier to understand through both visual and audio experiences. The project takes scientific data and converts it into sound. The resulting audio is then paired with its corresponding media data and stored. Visitors to the website can explore the prepared exhibits and play, pause and replay the audio. There will also be documentation explaining what each data property translates into as a sound characteristic.
The main beneficiaries of this project are visually impaired people, alongside people with Non-Verbal Learning Disability (NVLD) and Visual Processing Disorder (VPD), whom the project aims to support by providing an additional audio-based way to explore and understand information. Furthermore, the project offers people an interactive and fun way to engage with and understand the changes happening on Earth.
The technologies and tools we used are:
1. Python
2. NumPy
3. Pillow
4. JSON
5. React
6. HTML
7. CSS
8. JavaScript
9. NASA Earth Information Center (EIC) images
The creative aspect of the project is the combination of scientific visualization and sound characteristics. Our team considered the accuracy of the scientific information and the ease of navigation, since the main target audience includes visually impaired people.
details:
What does your project do or how does it work?

Earth Jukebox transforms scientific information from NASA Earth Information Center (EIC) images into an accessible digital experience. Our project processes NASA visual data and converts the information represented through images into structured data that can be explored through an interactive interface.

The image-processing pipeline uses Python, NumPy, Pillow, and JSON to load NASA images, process pixel and color information, divide images into spatial regions, and organize the extracted information into structured data. The React, HTML, CSS, and JavaScript interface provides the user-facing experience for interacting with the processed information.

Benefits

The main benefit of Earth Jukebox is making Earth science more accessible and easier to explore. Instead of relying only on traditional visual presentations, our project creates another way for users to interact with scientific information.

It can help users understand complex Earth data through a simpler, interactive experience and provides a foundation for making NASA scientific visualizations more inclusive.

What is the intended impact of the project?

Our goal is to make NASA Earth science more accessible to a wider audience, particularly by exploring ways of presenting visual scientific information in alternative formats.

We want Earth Jukebox to demonstrate how open NASA data can be transformed into accessible and interactive experiences. In the future, the concept could be expanded to support more types of Earth observations and more accessibility-focused ways of experiencing scientific data.

We developed the project using:

  • Python — image processing and data processing
  • NumPy — numerical and pixel-data processing
  • Pillow — loading and processing NASA images
  • JSON — storing structured image-processing results
  • React — building the interactive user interface
  • HTML — structuring the web interface
  • CSS — designing and styling the interface
  • JavaScript — implementing interactive functionality
  • NASA Earth Information Center (EIC) images — scientific source data for the project

The project was developed as a software-based solution without requiring specialized hardware.

Creativity In Our Project?

Earth Jukebox combines scientific data processing, accessibility, and interactive technology in one project. Instead of treating NASA images only as pictures, we process the visual information into structured data that software can understand and use.

The creative aspect is the idea of turning NASA's open Earth data into an experience that can be interacted with in a different way. This approach can help bridge the gap between complex scientific visualizations and users who may find traditional visual formats difficult to access.

Factors that our team considered

Our team considered several important factors while developing Earth Jukebox:

  • Accessibility — ensuring that scientific information can be experienced beyond traditional visual formats.
  • NASA data accuracy — using NASA Earth Information Center images as our scientific source.
  • Data processing — converting image information into structured, machine-readable data.
  • User experience — creating an interface that is simple and interactive.
  • Scalability — designing the project so that additional NASA Earth datasets and visualizations can be incorporated later.
  • Technology compatibility — combining Python-based data processing with a modern web interface using React, HTML, CSS, and JavaScript.
  • Open data — taking advantage of NASA's freely available Earth science resources to build a new application around them.

Overall, Earth Jukebox aims to turn NASA's open Earth data into a more accessible, interactive experience and demonstrate how technology can help more people engage with Earth science.
